newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia T-bills price fall seen too far too fast.
newsitem.headline: Russia T-bills price fall seen too far too fast.

text.p: Yields have plummeted too far too fast on Russia's booming domestic Treasury bill market, analysts said on Wednesday, predicting prices would come down soon.

Average market yields are down to about 20 percent, the level the Central Bank had forecast for year-end, falling from the high 20s early last month as the rouble has firmed and reformers have insisted they will clean up Russia's ramshackle economy.
"There is a bit of a bubble in the market," said Troika Dialog fixed income head Robert Devane. He said the bubble could be blown by even an slight signal that Russian risk was increasing

Analysts predicted yields could rise one to five percentage points in the short term if the Central Bank does not continue to support a strong rouble and foreigners do not accept that Russian risk has decreased enough to justify major investment at new, lower yields.
A 105-day bill was issued at an average yield of 18.87 percent on Wednesday. The closest maturity to the new issue had closed at 16.16 percent in secondary trade on Tuesday.
A 364-day bill, which as longer paper should attract more foreign interest, yielded 20.03 percent against 20.85 percent for the closest maturity in secondary trade on Tuesday.
"Foreign clients we speak to are very wary of this market," Devane said. "Fund investors are not necessarily convinced that Russia is a good buy on a risk-adjusted basis."

Russia has forecast the economy will shrink by two percent this year, revising earlier forecasts of two percent growth. The government also faces big budget and tax battles with a communist-dominated lower house of parliament.
Rinaco Plus fixed-income analyst Alexei Samoukov said the market was slightly overpriced on the expectation that the rouble will remain strong. He predicted yields would rise about a point.

The rouble has been strengthened by foreign flows and domestic demand, especially from delinquent tax payers. This was reflected in rising Central Bank foreign currency reserves, up by one third in May after doubling in April.

But Samoukov said the semi-independent Central Bank may allow the rouble to depreciate more steeply in order to help exporters and make it easier to pay pension arrears -- one of the government's top priorities.
"With the rouble depreciation much less than inflation (of 14.6 percent year on year in May), the efficiency of exports decreases," he said.
The forwards market, where many foreigners lock in yields on the rouble-denominated Treasury bills and bonds, was too optimistic about the chances of the rouble remaining strong, Samoukov said.

Forward rouble contracts were trading at about five percent annualised for six month contracts and about six percent for the year, he said, while the Central Bank has said depreciation this year is likely to be 8.6 percent.
If the rouble fell, foreigners who control up to 40 percent of the secondary market would require higher yields to lock in dollar-denominated returns.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell general manager Nick Jordan said foreign flows were coming in strongly and the 20 percent yield level was realistic by fundamental valuations. But some yield rise was possible for non-fundamental reasons.
"People will need to be convinced why it should go down through 20. It is a natural psychological barrier," he said, adding technicals pointed to a rise.
Jordan said investors would be watching the government's battles over 1997 spending cuts and a new tax code.
The market could respond well to increasing T-bill volumes at new low rates, if the issue was handled well. "Marketing is almost as important as fundamentals sometimes," he said.
